stem: If $X=\{-{=m}, \dots, -1, 0, 1, \dots, {=m}\}$ (all integers from $-{=m}$ to ${=m}$) and R is a relation on X where $a\,R\,b$ means: «The number a is the square of the number b» for each of $a, b\in X$. How many points does the cartesian diagram of R contain?
solution: The pair $(a, b)$ is in R when $a = b^2$ and both a and b belong to X.
Since $a = b^2$ must be at most {=m}, we need $b^2 \le {=m}$, so b can be any integer from $-{=r}$ to {=r}.
For each such b, $a=b^2$ is in X, so each gives exactly one pair $(b^2, b)$.
The number of values of b is $2\times{=r}+1={=c}$, so the cartesian diagram has {=c} points.
notes: Advanced twist: the relation is not one-to-one (b and -b give the same a), and pairs are ordered (a, b) with a the square. Count of b in [-r, r] with r=isqrt(m).
